messages:
Mia Chen: Quick heads-up — I found a reproducible long-context mem growth that looks tied to the continuous-batcher merge path + keycache reuse.
Sam Ortiz: Can you share the repro and any pprof output? :eyes:
Mia Chen: repro steps below. noticed mem climbs steadily after ~20k tokens on a single worker. attaching quick pprof snapshot.
```
# repro (run on debug build, small cluster)
python tools/repro_longctx.py --model redwood-7b --seq 32 --long-context 8192 --load-pattern mix
# then: go tool pprof -http=localhost:6060 cpu.pprof
```
Mia Chen: pprof heap snapshot snippet:
```
10.3MB  42.1% 42.1%  runtime.makeslice
4.5MB  18.4% 60.5%  github.com/redwood/inference/kv.(*Cache).AllocateFragment
3.2MB  13.1% 73.6%  github.com/redwood/inference/serving/contbatch.mergeBatches
2.1MB   8.6% 82.2%  github.com/redwood/inference/kv.(*Cache).EvictCandidate
```
Arpan Rao: Interesting — `mergeBatches` showing up in heap means merged requests are keeping KV fragments alive longer than expected. sounds like ownership/seq-range rounding isn't matching eviction boundaries.
Lina Vega: Is this only when seq lengths are mixed? We saw fragmentation before with mid/long combos.
Mia Chen: Yes, worst with mixed seqs (32 + 2048) in same merge. small batches first, then merged behind a long request -> head-of-line effect.
Sam Ortiz: Could be the batcher merging incompatible `kv_owner` ranges. If merge picks winner request's owner, others' fragments become sticky and cannot be reclaimed until whole merged KV life ends. That explains steady growth.
Taylor Green: FYI I pushed a kernel selection change last week (PR #1423) that tightened fused-attn path. Might have affected how we pin KV slot lifetimes (changed allocation alignment). Could be related.
perf-bot: Deploy notice: PR #1423 deployed to staging at 2026-03-16T04:12:00Z
Arpan Rao: Two quick ideas: 1) in `mergeBatches` only merge if `kv_owner` match OR simulated reuse score > 0.8; 2) add reference-counted fragment view to allow partial reclaim when prefix not observed.
Lina Vega: I'm in favor of the heuristic gate first — low risk. we can roll it behind a flag.
Sam Ortiz: I'll prototype a gate where we compute prefix-match ratio across requests. pseudocode:
```go
func shouldMerge(a, b *Request) bool {
  score := prefixMatchRatio(a.KVKeys, b.KVKeys)
  return score >= 0.8 && a.TailLen < maxTail && b.TailLen < maxTail
}
```
Mia Chen: Also adding a short-term mitigator: force per-fragment TTL on merge if seq disparity > 4x. cheap, safe.
Taylor Green: If we add TTL on merged fragments, check perf for small-latency regressions. the kernel change already impacted hot-path L1 usage in microbench.
Sam Ortiz: I'll run a microbenchmark matrix: with/without gate, with/without TTL, with PR#1423 kernel. will post numbers.
Mia Chen: Thanks. next steps: Sam to bench + attach flamegraphs, Arpan to spec the gate + flag, Lina to add unit tests for merge ordering, Taylor to review interaction with kernel change.
Sam Ortiz: quick note: I saw a repro variant where eviction candidates spike but eviction loop fails to reclaim because `fragment.owner` pointer swapped during merge — adding test for stable owner pointers. :thumbsup:
Mia Chen: Great. I'll add a short long-run smoke job to CI to catch the steady growth (20k token window). tagging infra to schedule. :pray:
Lina Vega: ping @perf-bot when benchmarks are ready so we can auto-collect traces.
perf-bot: Ack — will collect and post perf artifacts to /artifacts/1965432100/
Mia Chen: Thanks all — moving this to a small RFC doc in PR soon.
